questions.stem: How do the particles in a solid move?

options.text: they vibrate about fixed positions
options.explanation: Fixed sites plus vibration is the signature of the solid state.

options.text: they slide past one another freely
options.explanation: Sliding neighbours describe a liquid, where positions are not fixed.

options.text: they fly around at high speed in all directions
options.explanation: Free flight between collisions describes a gas.

options.text: they stay completely still at all temperatures
options.explanation: Particles always carry some vibration above absolute zero.

questions.stem: Which property does a liquid share with a solid?

options.text: particles flying between distant collisions
options.explanation: That is gaseous behaviour; liquid neighbours stay in contact.

options.text: a fixed volume
options.explanation: Particles remain in contact in both states, so neither is readily compressed.

options.text: a fixed shape of its own
options.explanation: Only the solid holds its own shape; a liquid adopts its container's.

options.text: particles locked in a regular pattern
options.explanation: Regular packing belongs to the solid lattice only.

questions.stem: Why does a liquid take the shape of the bottom of its container?

options.text: its particles are locked in place so gravity pulls the whole block down
options.explanation: Locked particles would preserve the original shape, as in a solid.

options.text: its particles shrink so the liquid collapses
options.explanation: Particle size never changes between states; only spacing and motion do.

options.text: its particles can move past one another while staying in contact
options.explanation: Relative sliding lets the bulk flow until it settles under gravity.

options.text: its particles expand to fill the whole container
options.explanation: Liquids keep a fixed volume; only gases fill the space available.

questions.stem: Which statement about the spacing of particles is correct for solids and liquids?

options.text: liquid particles are far apart like a gas
options.explanation: Large separations appear only in the gas state.

options.text: solid particles have big gaps that lock them apart
options.explanation: Solids are the most tightly packed of the three states.

options.text: particle spacing is identical in all three states
options.explanation: Spacing widens dramatically only on vaporisation.

options.text: particles touch in both states, with a liquid only slightly less dense
options.explanation: Both states are close-packed; melting costs little volume for most substances.

questions.stem: A block of ice is dropped into a jug and melts. What has changed for its particles?

options.text: they kept touching but gained the ability to slide past each other
options.explanation: Melting moves particles from fixed lattice sites to mobile contact — the liquid signature.

options.text: they moved far apart and fly independently
options.explanation: That describes boiling to a gas, not melting to a liquid.

options.text: they became smaller and packed tighter
options.explanation: Particle size is fixed; melting slightly loosens the packing.

options.text: nothing changed because the substance is still water
options.explanation: Same substance, different state — the arrangement and motion did change.

questions.stem: State the arrangement and motion of particles in a solid.
questions.modelAnswer: Solid particles are packed in a regular, fixed arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions without changing places.

questions.stem: State two bulk properties that a liquid has but a gas does not.
questions.modelAnswer: A liquid keeps a fixed volume and sits in contact at the bottom of the container, whereas a gas expands to fill all the space available.

questions.stem: Explain why a solid keeps its own shape when it is tipped out of a mould but a liquid does not.
questions.modelAnswer: In the solid each particle is locked to one site in a regular lattice, so the relative positions of all the particles cannot change and the moulded shape survives. In a liquid the particles remain in contact but can slide past one another, so the collection flows under gravity and adopts the shape of the surface that holds it.

questions.stem: A student tips 200 cm3 of liquid from a bottle into a wide dish. State what happens to the volume of the liquid and use particle behaviour to explain the shape it ends up with.
questions.modelAnswer: The volume stays 200 cm3 because liquid particles remain in contact, so the substance is neither compressed nor expanded. The particles slide past one another, so the liquid spreads until it forms a shallow layer taking the shape of the dish bottom.

questions.stem: Which description matches the particles of a gas?

options.text: arranged in a regular pattern with large gaps
options.explanation: Gas arrangements are irregular as well as widely separated.

options.text: far apart, moving fast and randomly in all directions
options.explanation: Large separations and rapid random motion define the gas state.

options.text: touching, vibrating about fixed points
options.explanation: That is the solid arrangement.

options.text: touching but sliding past each other
options.explanation: That is the liquid arrangement.

questions.stem: What can be said about the shape and volume of a gas?

options.text: fixed volume, fixed shape
options.explanation: That pair describes a solid.

options.text: fixed volume, variable shape
options.explanation: That pair describes a liquid.

options.text: both shape and volume change to match the container
options.explanation: Free flight between collisions lets the gas occupy all available space.

options.text: fixed shape, variable volume
options.explanation: No state pairs a fixed shape with a variable volume.

questions.stem: Why does a gas spread out to fill the whole container?

options.text: its particles attract each other into every corner
options.explanation: Inter-particle forces in a gas are negligible between collisions.

options.text: its particles grow in size until they touch every wall
options.explanation: Particle size never changes; only separation does.

options.text: gravity pulls them evenly across the container
options.explanation: Filling is uniform precisely because gravity is not the driver at particle scale.

options.text: its particles travel in straight lines between collisions with nothing holding them together
options.explanation: Unconstrained straight-line motion carries particles to every region of the space.

questions.stem: A sealed syringe contains air. The plunger is pushed in and the air is squeezed into half the volume. Which particle property made this possible?

options.text: the large empty separations between gas particles
options.explanation: Most of a gas is empty space, so particles can be forced closer.

options.text: the particles themselves shrank
options.explanation: Particle size is fixed; only the separations reduce.

options.text: the regular arrangement collapsed
options.explanation: Gases have no regular arrangement to begin with.

options.text: some particles escaped through the syringe
options.explanation: The syringe is sealed, so the particle count is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which row correctly links each state to its particle behaviour?

options.text: all three states vibrate about fixed points
options.explanation: Only the solid locks particles to sites.

options.text: solid vibrate in place, liquid slide in contact, gas fly freely apart
options.explanation: Each state is correctly paired with its particle freedom.

options.text: solid slide in contact, liquid vibrate in place, gas fly freely apart
options.explanation: The solid and liquid behaviours are swapped.

options.text: solid vibrate in place, liquid fly freely apart, gas slide in contact
options.explanation: The liquid and gas behaviours are swapped.

questions.stem: State the arrangement and motion of particles in a gas.
questions.modelAnswer: Gas particles are widely separated with no regular arrangement, moving rapidly and randomly in all directions between collisions.

questions.stem: State what happens to the shape and the volume of a gas released into a larger container.
questions.modelAnswer: Both increase: the gas takes the shape of the new container and its volume grows to fill all of the space available.

questions.stem: Explain why the same substance can hold a fixed volume as a liquid but a variable volume as a gas.
questions.modelAnswer: Liquid particles remain in contact, so pushing them appreciably closer is resisted by the contact forces and the volume is effectively fixed. In a gas the particles are already far apart with negligible binding between them, so there is abundant empty space and nothing prevents the separations growing or shrinking, letting the volume match whatever container holds it.

questions.stem: A balloon is filled with air and placed inside a vacuum chamber from which the outside pressure is removed. Use the particle model to explain what happens to the balloon's volume.
questions.modelAnswer: Inside the balloon the air particles keep colliding with the inner walls and push outward. With the outside pressure removed there is less inward push on the rubber, so the balloon expands until the rubber's tension balances the particle collisions — its volume increases because gas particles fly freely and fill the larger space.
